newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to complain to WTO over Indonesia car policy.
newsitem.headline: Japan to complain to WTO over Indonesia car policy.

text.p: Japan announced on Wednesday that it would complain to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) over Indonesia's national car policy, forming a united front with its traditional trade adversary, the United States.

Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) said Japan plans to file complaint with WTO over the issue "within a week or so", but Tokyo ruled out using trade or aid retaliation measures as a way to settle the dispute.

"There is a strong suspicion that Indonesia's national car policy contravenes WTO rules. We are very concerned, and we have been repeatedly expressing our fears to (Indonesia's) President Suharto," government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told reporters.
In Jakarta, Indonesian Trade and Industry Minister Tunky Ariwibowo said Indonesia was ready to argue its case.
"We are ready to face the WTO," he told reporters. "We will hire laywers."
Japan's MITI said it had confirmed Indonesia had not imposed any tariffs on its "national" cars produced in South Korea when they passed through Indonesian customs.
"As soon as we confirm the number and sales price of these cars, we will start the procedures for filing a complaint to the WTO within a week or so," a ministry official told reporters.
Indonesia's national car plan, announced earlier this year, has come under fire from Japan, the United States and the European Union as a violation of world trade rules.
Indonesia said in February that a firm controlled by President Suharto's youngest son, Hutomo Mandala Putra, would get tax breaks to manufacture sedans in collaboration with South Korea's Kia Motors.

The company, PT Timor Putra Nasional, is the only firm granted this privilege. It must raise local content to 60 percent within three years of starting up but has been allowed to import an initial batch of cars duty-free from South Korea.
The first consignment of cars arrived in Jakarta last month. Japan argues the special tax treatment breaches WTO rules and puts rival manufacturers at a disadvantage.

Industry sources in Japan say Japanese makers currently enjoy a 95 percent share of the Indonesian vehicle market through joint-venture assembly and licensing arrangements with local firms and view the national car project as a threat to this status.
But Tokyo -- the biggest aid donor country to Indonesia -- said it would not use trade or aid retaliatory steps to press Jakarta for a quick solution.

"We hope the car issue does not sour our ties with Indonesia. We are not planning to take any retaliatory trade measures or connect this with our aid policy," another MITI official said. "We want to settle this through dialogue."

On Tuesday, Washington warned that Indonesia's policies of granting tax and tariff benefits to "national car" makers based on the percentage of domestic content in their vehicles would also be subject to a U.S. complaint to the WTO.

Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky told a news conference that the car issue would also be subject to investigations under the so-called Section 301 U.S. trade law that allows retaliation against unfair practices.
As well as the joint ventures, Japan also exported 36,000 cars worth about $247 million to Indonesia in 1995. Officials did not say how much exports would be hurt by the new policy.
Yoshifumi Tsuji, chairman of the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association, said it was "regrettable Indonesia has implemented trade benefits which clearly go against WTO rules.
"I hope government-level talks will lead to a quick solution," he added.
